claim: Kindlin-1 is over-expressed in breast cancer where it is associated with metastasis-free survival.
source: The adhesion protein Kindlin-1 is over-expressed in breast cancer where it is associated with metastasis-free survival; however, the mechanisms involved are poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Azorin et al., 2018; Sin et al., 2011) as mentioned in the Introduction section.

claim: Deletion of Kindlin-1 in Met-1 mammary tumor cells led to tumor regression following injection into immunocompetent hosts.
source: Deletion of Kindlin-1 in Met-1 mammary tumor cells led to tumor regression following injection into immunocompetent hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D, demonstrating complete tumor regression by day 19 in FVB mice.

claim: Deletion of Kindlin-1 was associated with a reduction in tumor infiltrating Tregs.
source: This was associated with a reduction in tumor infiltrating Tregs.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3A showing reduced Treg percentages in Kin1-NULL tumors.

claim: There was a significant increase in IL-6 secretion from Met-1 cells when Kindlin-1 was depleted.
source: There was a significant increase in IL-6 secretion from Met-1 cells when Kindlin-1 was depleted and conditioned media from Kindlin-1-depleted cells led to a decrease in the ability of Tregs to suppress the proliferation of CD8+ T cells, which was dependent on IL-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5B and protein array data in Figure 5A.

claim: Conditioned media from Kindlin-1-depleted cells led to a decrease in the ability of Tregs to suppress the proliferation of CD8+ T cells, which was dependent on IL-6.
source: There was a significant increase in IL-6 secretion from Met-1 cells when Kindlin-1 was depleted and conditioned media from Kindlin-1-depleted cells led to a decrease in the ability of Tregs to suppress the proliferation of CD8+ T cells, which was dependent on IL-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by Treg suppression assay data shown in Figure 6I and J, demonstrating IL-6 blocking antibody reversed the effect.

claim: Deletion of tumor-derived IL-6 in the Kindlin-1-depleted tumors reversed the reduction of tumor-infiltrating Tregs.
source: In addition, deletion of tumor-derived IL-6 in the Kindlin-1-depleted tumors reversed the reduction of tumor-infiltrating Tregs.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A comparing Kin1-NULL IL-6-CTRL and Kin1-NULL IL-6-NULL tumors.

claim: Kindlin-1 localises to focal adhesions where it plays an important role in controlling integrin activation via binding to integrin β subunits.
source: Kindlin-1 is a four-point-one, ezrin, radixin, moesin (FERM) domain-containing adaptor protein that localises to focal adhesions, where it plays an important role in controlling integrin activation via binding to integrin β subunits (Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rognoni et al., 2016.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1 leads to Kindler Syndrome.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding Kindlin-1, FERMT1, leads to Kindler Syndrome, a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis that causes skin atrophy, blistering, photosensitivity, hyper or hypo-pigmentation, increased light sensitivity and an enhanced risk of developing aggressive squamous cell carcinoma (Guerrero-Aspizua et al., 2019; Lai-Cheong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guerrero-Aspizua et al., 2019 and Lai-Cheong et al., 2009.

claim: Kindlin-1 expression is higher in tumor versus normal breast tissue.
source: In breast cancer, Kindlin-1 expression is higher in tumor versus normal breast tissue and its expression is associated with metastasis-free survival (Azorin et al., 2018; Sin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Azorin et al., 2018 and Sin et al., 2011.

claim: Kindlin-1 controls both breast cancer cell adhesion, migration and invasion.
source: Consistent with its recognised role in regulating integrin-extracellular matrix interactions, Kindlin-1 controls both breast cancer cell adhesion, migration and invasion (Azorin et al., 2018; Sarvi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Azorin et al., 2018 and Sarvi et al., 2018.

claim: Kindlin-1 regulates TGFβ signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in breast cancer.
source: Kindlin-1 also regulates TGFβ signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in breast cancer (Sin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sin et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 significantly delays tumor onset and reduces the incidence of lung metastasis in the PyV MT-driven mouse model of mammary tumorigenesis.
source: We have previously shown in the polyomavirus middle T antigen (PyV MT)-driven mouse model of mammary tumorigenesis, that loss of Kindlin-1 significantly delays tumor onset and reduces the incidence of lung metastasis (Sarvi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sarvi et al., 2018.

claim: Kindlin-1 stimulates metastatic growth via integrin-dependent adhesion of circulating tumor cells to endothelial cells in the metastatic niche.
source: Mechanistically, Kindlin-1 stimulates metastatic growth in this model via integrin-dependent adhesion of circulating tumor cells to endothelial cells in the metastatic niche (Sarvi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sarvi et al., 2018.

claim: A number of pro-inflammatory cytokines are upregulated in the skin of Kindler syndrome patients.
source: Kindlin-1 has also been shown to regulate inflammation in the skin of Kindler syndrome patients, where a number of pro-inflammatory cytokines are upregulated (Heinemann et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2016), and increased expression of genes associated with cytokine signaling have been reported (Chacón-Solano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heinemann et al., 2011 and Maier et al., 2016.

claim: Increased expression of genes associated with cytokine signaling have been reported in Kindler Syndrome.
source: Kindlin-1 has also been shown to regulate inflammation in the skin of Kindler syndrome patients, where a number of pro-inflammatory cytokines are upregulated (Heinemann et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2016), and increased expression of genes associated with cytokine signaling have been reported (Chacón-Solano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chacón-Solano et al., 2019.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 led to reduced tumor growth in CD-1 nude mice.
source: Loss of Kindlin-1 led to reduced tumor growth in CD-1 nude mice (Figure 1A and B) with significant differences in tumor size noted from day 10 onwards.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Significant differences in tumor size were noted from day 10 onwards in CD-1 nude mice injected with Kin1-NULL cells.
source: Loss of Kindlin-1 led to reduced tumor growth in CD-1 nude mice (Figure 1A and B) with significant differences in tumor size noted from day 10 onwards.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A similar reduced tumor growth rate in CD1 nude mice was seen following injection of human MDA-MB-231 cells in which Kindlin-1 was depleted using shRNA.
source: A similar reduced tumor growth rate in CD1 nude mice was seen following injection of human MDA-MB-231 cells in which Kindlin-1 was depleted using shRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 had no effect on in vitro cell proliferation.
source: In both cell models loss of Kindlin-1 had no effect on in vitro cell proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), while immunohistochemical analysis of Ki67 and phospho-histone H3 in tumors showed there was no effect on proliferation in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis of Ki67 and phospho-histone H3 in tumors showed there was no effect on proliferation in vivo.
source: In both cell models loss of Kindlin-1 had no effect on in vitro cell proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), while immunohistochemical analysis of Ki67 and phospho-histone H3 in tumors showed there was no effect on proliferation in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When Met-1 cells were injected into immune competent FVB mice, there was complete tumor regression by day 19.
source: In contrast when Met-1 cells were injected into immune competent FVB mice, although Kindlin-1 loss led to a similar delay in tumor growth at day 10, there was complete tumor regression by day 19 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Kindlin-1 is required for tumor growth of Met-1 cells in mice with a functional immune system.
source: Thus, Kindlin-1 is required for tumor growth of Met-1 cells in mice with a functional immune system, similar to what we reported previously for FAK-deficiency in a mouse model of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) (Serrels et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and D, and inference from comparison to prior work.

claim: Growth of the Kin1-AA mutant-expressing tumors was indistinguishable from Kin1-WT tumors in both CD1 nude and FVB mice.
source: Growth of the Kin1-AA mutant-expressing tumors was indistinguishable from Kin1-WT tumors in both CD1 nude and FVB mice (Figure 1A and C respectively), implying that integrin dependent functions of Kindlin-1 are not important for the growth of Met-1 tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: Integrin dependent functions of Kindlin-1 are not important for the growth of Met-1 tumors.
source: Growth of the Kin1-AA mutant-expressing tumors was indistinguishable from Kin1-WT tumors in both CD1 nude and FVB mice (Figure 1A and C respectively), implying that integrin dependent functions of Kindlin-1 are not important for the growth of Met-1 tumors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Kin1-AA tumors grow similarly to Kin1-WT tumors.

claim: Neither Kin1-WT nor Kin1-NULL cells grew palpable tumors in mice which had been pre-challenged with Kin1-NULL cells.
source: Neither Kin1-WT nor Kin1-NULL cells grew palpable tumors in mice which had been pre-challenged with Kin1-NULL cells, while injection of Kin1-WT or Kin1-NULL cells into naive mice on the same day showed normal tumor growth and survival (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Injection of Kin1-WT or Kin1-NULL cells into naive mice showed normal tumor growth and survival.
source: Neither Kin1-WT nor Kin1-NULL cells grew palpable tumors in mice which had been pre-challenged with Kin1-NULL cells, while injection of Kin1-WT or Kin1-NULL cells into naive mice on the same day showed normal tumor growth and survival (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Deletion of Kindlin-1 promotes effective immunosurveillance, resulting in tumor regression and lasting immunological memory.
source: These data suggest that deletion of Kindlin-1 promotes effective immunosurveillance, resulting in tumor regression and lasting immunological memory.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the re-challenge experiment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Kindlin-1 does not regulate key antigens permitting T-cell tumor recognition and effective immunosurveillance.
source: Furthermore, the inability of Kin1-WT cells to give rise to tumors in mice previously harbouring a Kin1-NULL tumor suggests that Kindlin-1 does not regulate key antigens permitting T-cell tumor recognition and effective immunosurveillance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that pre-challenged mice reject both Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors.

claim: There were significantly reduced CD45+ cells within Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Of note there were significantly reduced CD45+ cells within Kin1-NULL tumors, alongside a reduction in both monocytes and macrophages (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a reduction in both monocytes and macrophages in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Of note there were significantly reduced CD45+ cells within Kin1-NULL tumors, alongside a reduction in both monocytes and macrophages (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No significant differences were observed in expression of the phenotype markers MHC II, CD206 and SIRPα, between Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumor-associated macrophages.
source: However, no significant differences were observed in expression of the phenotype markers MHC II, CD206 and SIRPα, between Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumor-associated macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that there is no change in the 'polarisation' status of these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is no change in the 'polarisation' status of macrophages in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: However, no significant differences were observed in expression of the phenotype markers MHC II, CD206 and SIRPα, between Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumor-associated macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that there is no change in the 'polarisation' status of these cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of change in polarization markers.

claim: There was a significant increase in conventional type I DCs (cDC1) within Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT.
source: Although there was no difference in total dendritic cell (DC) percentages, analysis of DC subsets demonstrated a significant increase in conventional type I DCs (cDC1) within Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: cDC1s are efficient at cross presentation, essential for CD8+ responses and have been demonstrated to be important for anti-tumor immune responses.
source: cDC1s are efficient at cross presentation, essential for CD8+ responses and have been demonstrated to be important for anti-tumor immune responses (Ferris et al., 2020; Laoui et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferris et al., 2020 and Laoui et al., 2016.

claim: There was increased expression of the T-cell co-stimulatory molecule CD80 on DCs in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Furthermore, we observed increased expression of the T-cell co-stimulatory molecule CD80 on DCs in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and increased expression of the T cell inhibitory PD-1 receptor ligand PD-L1 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was increased expression of the T cell inhibitory PD-1 receptor ligand PD-L1 on DCs in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Furthermore, we observed increased expression of the T-cell co-stimulatory molecule CD80 on DCs in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and increased expression of the T cell inhibitory PD-1 receptor ligand PD-L1 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Analysis of bulk tumor RNA demonstrated an increase in antigen presentation (H2-Q2 and H2-Eb1) and antigen transport (Tap2) related genes within Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Additionally, analysis of bulk tumor RNA demonstrated an increase in antigen presentation (H2-Q2 and H2-Eb1) and antigen transport (Tap2) related genes within Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: An increase in Ifng was seen in the Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: An increase in Ifng was also seen in the Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 2G), consistent with increased expression of IFNγ-inducible PD-L1, and MHC/Antigen processing genes (Zhou, 2009; Garcia-Diaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The increase in Ifng is consistent with increased expression of IFNγ-inducible PD-L1, and MHC/Antigen processing genes.
source: An increase in Ifng was also seen in the Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 2G), consistent with increased expression of IFNγ-inducible PD-L1, and MHC/Antigen processing genes (Zhou, 2009; Garcia-Diaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou, 2009 and Garcia-Diaz et al., 2017, and inference from the data.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 may result in increased cross-presentation of tumor antigen by DCs, promoting T-cell activation and anti-tumor immunity.
source: These data suggest that loss of Kindlin-1 may result in increased cross-presentation of tumor antigen by DCs, promoting T-cell activation and anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed increases in cDC1 cells, CD80, and antigen presentation genes.

claim: Overall PD-L1 gene (Cd274) expression was found to be decreased on CD45+ cells isolated from both tumors and draining lymph nodes (dLN) of Kin1-NULL tumors, compared to Kin1-WT tumors.
source: Despite an increase in PD-L1 protein expression noted on cDC1 cells, overall PD-L1 gene (Cd274) expression was found to be decreased on CD45+ cells isolated from both tumors and draining lymph nodes (dLN) of Kin1-NULL tumors, compared to Kin1-WT tumors, although this did not reach significance in the tumors (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Analysis of a publicly available human breast cancer data set (METABRIC), demonstrated a small but significant correlation between FERMT1 (Kindlin-1) and CD274 (PD-L1) gene expression.
source: Analysis of a publicly available human breast cancer data set (METABRIC), demonstrated a small but significant correlation between FERMT1 (Kindlin-1) and CD274 (PD-L1) gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 can lead to modulation of PD-L1 expression on tumor infiltrating immune cells.
source: Together these data show that loss of Kindlin-1 can lead to modulation of PD-L1 expression on tumor infiltrating immune cells, suggesting that the PD-1/L1 pathway may contribute to the anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in PD-L1 expression.

claim: The PD-1/L1 pathway may contribute to the anti-tumor immune response in Kindlin-1-deficient tumors.
source: Together these data show that loss of Kindlin-1 can lead to modulation of PD-L1 expression on tumor infiltrating immune cells, suggesting that the PD-1/L1 pathway may contribute to the anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the observed PD-L1 modulation.

claim: There was a significant reduction of total CD3+ cells in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: We found a significant reduction of total CD3+ cells in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which was driven by a decrease in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The reduction of total CD3+ cells in Kin1-NULL tumors was driven by a decrease in CD4+ T cells.
source: We found a significant reduction of total CD3+ cells in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which was driven by a decrease in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the flow cytometry data.

claim: There was a significant decrease of regulatory T (Treg) cells as a percentage of total cells in Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT tumors.
source: Within the CD4+ cell compartment, a significant decrease of regulatory T (Treg) cells as a percentage of total cells was evident in Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT tumors (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduction of Tregs was also observed when analysing cells as a percentage of total CD3+ cells.
source: The reduction of Tregs was also observed when analysing cells as a percentage of total CD3+ cells, with a significant increase in non-Treg CD4+ cells as a proportion of total CD3+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was a significant increase in non-Treg CD4+ cells as a proportion of total CD3+ in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: The reduction of Tregs was also observed when analysing cells as a percentage of total CD3+ cells, with a significant increase in non-Treg CD4+ cells as a proportion of total CD3+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Treg cells are widely reported to control anti-tumor T cell responses.
source: As Treg cells are widely reported to control anti-tumor T cell responses (Hatzioannou et al., 2021), these data suggest that Kindlin-1 loss results in fewer infiltrating suppressive T cells within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hatzioannou et al., 2021.

claim: Kindlin-1 loss results in fewer infiltrating suppressive T cells within the tumor microenvironment.
source: As Treg cells are widely reported to control anti-tumor T cell responses (Hatzioannou et al., 2021), these data suggest that Kindlin-1 loss results in fewer infiltrating suppressive T cells within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed reduction in Tregs.

claim: The reduction in Tregs was mirrored in the tumor draining lymph nodes of Kin1-NULL tumors at day 10.
source: Furthermore, the reduction in Tregs was mirrored in the tumor draining lymph nodes of Kin1-NULL tumors at day 10, but not observed systemically in the spleen (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The reduction in Tregs was not observed systemically in the spleen.
source: Furthermore, the reduction in Tregs was mirrored in the tumor draining lymph nodes of Kin1-NULL tumors at day 10, but not observed systemically in the spleen (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The reduction in Tregs is due to changes in the local tumor environment.
source: This suggests that the reduction in Tregs is due to changes in the local tumor environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Treg reduction is local, not systemic.

claim: An increase in naïve (CD62L+ CD44-) CD8+ cells was observed in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: We found no significant changes in memory marker expression on non-Treg CD4+ cells; however, an increase in naïve (CD62L+ CD44-) CD8+ cells was observed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant increase in CD62L+ Treg cells within Kin1-NULL tumors when compared to Kin1-WT tumors at day 10.
source: Interestingly, a significant increase in CD62L+ Treg cells was evident within Kin1-NULL tumors when compared to Kin1-WT tumors at day 10 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A corresponding reduction in CD62L- Treg proportions were noted in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: A corresponding reduction in CD62L- Treg proportions were also noted.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the flow cytometry data in Figure 3C.

claim: CD62L+ Treg cells have been categorised into resting Tregs, with reduced proliferative capacity.
source: CD62L+ Treg cells have been categorised into resting Tregs, with reduced proliferative capacity, whereas CD62L- populations are reported to be activated Tregs with increased suppressive capacity, and accumulation of these cells into tumors drives CD8+ T cell suppression (Luo et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019; Huehn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019; Huehn et al., 2004.

claim: CD62L- populations are reported to be activated Tregs with increased suppressive capacity, and accumulation of these cells into tumors drives CD8+ T cell suppression.
source: CD62L+ Treg cells have been categorised into resting Tregs, with reduced proliferative capacity, whereas CD62L- populations are reported to be activated Tregs with increased suppressive capacity, and accumulation of these cells into tumors drives CD8+ T cell suppression (Luo et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019; Huehn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019; Huehn et al., 2004.

claim: The switch in the prominence of CD62L+ and CD62L- Treg subsets in the Kin1-NULL tumors suggests that more resting Tregs are present compared to Kin1-WT tumors.
source: The switch in the prominence of these two subsets in the Kin1-NULL tumors suggests that more resting Tregs are present compared to Kin1-WT tumors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in CD62L+ and CD62L- Treg proportions.

claim: There was a reduction of double positive (exhaustion) cells within CD4mem and TregCD62L+ populations in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Of note, a reduction of double positive (exhaustion) cells within CD4mem and TregCD62L+ populations was seen in Kin1-NULL tumors, alongside a corresponding increase in double negative (PD-1- TIM-3-) cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was a corresponding increase in double negative (PD-1- TIM-3-) cells in CD4mem and TregCD62L+ populations in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Of note, a reduction of double positive (exhaustion) cells within CD4mem and TregCD62L+ populations was seen in Kin1-NULL tumors, alongside a corresponding increase in double negative (PD-1- TIM-3-) cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 in Met-1 tumors is primarily modulating CD4+ T cell phenotypes, specifically that of Tregs.
source: These data suggest that loss of Kindlin-1 in Met-1 tumors is primarily modulating CD4+ T cell phenotypes, specifically that of Tregs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in Treg phenotypes.

claim: There was an increase of cDC1 cells in tumors from the MT-Kin-1fl/fl mice when compared to tumors in the MT-Kin-1wt/wt mice.
source: We observed an increase of cDC1 cells in tumors from the MT-Kin-1fl/fl mice when compared to tumors in the MT-Kin-1wt/wt mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), similar to the Met-1 cell-line-derived tumors already described (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There was a reduction of PD-L1 expression on CD45+ cells in MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors.
source: Furthermore, there was a reduction of PD-L1 expression on CD45+ cells in MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), as well as reduced PD-L1 on several myeloid subsets, demonstrating modulation of the PD-L1 pathway in Kindlin-1-deficient tumors also in this spontaneous breast cancer model.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There was reduced PD-L1 on several myeloid subsets in MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors.
source: Furthermore, there was a reduction of PD-L1 expression on CD45+ cells in MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), as well as reduced PD-L1 on several myeloid subsets, demonstrating modulation of the PD-L1 pathway in Kindlin-1-deficient tumors also in this spontaneous breast cancer model.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors had significantly fewer Treg cells with an increase in percentage of non-Treg CD4+ cells when analyzed as a percentage of total CD3+ cells.
source: However, when analyzed as a percentage of total CD3+ cells, MT-Kin-1fl/fl tumors had significantly fewer Treg cells with an increase in percentage of non-Treg CD4+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), that was similar to the Met-1 cell-line-derived tumor model (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Immune modulation upon the loss of Kindlin-1 tumor expression occurs in distinct models of breast cancer, with consistent changes in Treg and cDC1 cells resulting from Kindlin deficiency.
source: These data demonstrate immune modulation upon the loss of Kindlin-1 tumor expression in distinct models of breast cancer, with consistent changes in Treg and cDC1 cells resulting from Kindlin deficiency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of Met-1 and MMTV-PyV MT models.

claim: In the MT-Kin-1fl/fl mice we do not see tumor regression, which most likely reflects the incomplete loss of Kindlin-1 in the mammary tumor cells in this model.
source: However, in the MT-Kin-1fl/fl mice we do not see tumor regression, which most likely reflects the incomplete loss of Kindlin-1 in the mammary tumor cells in this model (Sarvi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of no tumor regression and citation to prior work.

claim: Analysis of RNA from CD45+ tumor infiltrating cells isolated from Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors showed a reduction of various T cell inhibitory checkpoint pathway related genes, including Cd274, Vsir and Havcr2 in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Analysis of RNA from CD45+ tumor infiltrating cells isolated from Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors was carried out which showed a reduction of various T cell inhibitory checkpoint pathway related genes, including Cd274, Vsir and Havcr2 in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Downregulation of TNF superfamily co-stimulatory receptors GITR, 4-1BB and OX40 was observed in Kin1-NULL infiltrating Tregs.
source: Of note, downregulation of TNF superfamily co-stimulatory receptors GITR, 4-1BB and OX40 was observed in Kin1-NULL infiltrating Tregs (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, D), which are critical for Treg development and promoting their proliferation (Willoughby et al., 2017; Alissafi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, D.

claim: GITR, 4-1BB and OX40 are critical for Treg development and promoting their proliferation.
source: Of note, downregulation of TNF superfamily co-stimulatory receptors GITR, 4-1BB and OX40 was observed in Kin1-NULL infiltrating Tregs (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, D), which are critical for Treg development and promoting their proliferation (Willoughby et al., 2017; Alissafi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Willoughby et al., 2017 and Alissafi et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of the inhibitory receptors LAG-3, CTLA-4, TIGIT and PD-1 were downregulated on the surface of Tregs in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Expression of the inhibitory receptors LAG-3, CTLA-4, TIGIT and PD-1 were also downregulated on the surface of Tregs in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D.

claim: LAG-3, CTLA-4, TIGIT and PD-1 receptors are crucial for Treg differentiation and immunosuppressive activity.
source: Although ligation of these receptors in CD8+ and non-Treg CD4+ cells inhibits effector function, these receptors are crucial for Treg differentiation and immunosuppressive activity (Alissafi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alissafi et al., 2019.

claim: There was significant downregulation of both CD73 and CD39 expression on Tregs from Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: There was significant downregulation of both CD73 and CD39 expression on Tregs from Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The CD39/CD73 pathway is a major modulator of Treg activity via metabolism of ATP to create extracellular adenosine, in turn inhibiting effector T cell function.
source: The CD39/CD73 pathway is a major modulator of Treg activity via metabolism of ATP to create extracellular adenosine, in turn inhibiting effector T cell function (Antonioli et al., 2013; Allard et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antonioli et al., 2013 and Allard et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 may cause metabolic changes in Treg cells, resulting in impairment of their suppressive capacity.
source: This suggests that loss of Kindlin-1 may cause metabolic changes in Treg cells, resulting in impairment of their suppressive capacity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed downregulation of CD73 and CD39.

claim: There was no overt modulation of Treg proliferation in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: Despite these phenotypic changes, there was no overt modulation of Treg proliferation seen (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Downregulation of phenotypic markers suggests that Tregs from Kin-1 NULL tumors could be less immunosuppressive, and therefore allow development of a sufficient anti-tumor immune response, leading to tumor clearance.
source: Taken together, downregulation of these phenotypic markers suggests that Tregs from Kin-1 NULL tumors could be less immunosuppressive, and therefore allow development of a sufficient anti-tumor immune response, leading to tumor clearance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed phenotypic changes in Tregs.

claim: There was an increase in expression of OX40, CD83 and CD29 on CD8+ T cells infiltrating Kin1-NULL tumors compared to those in Kin1-WT tumors.
source: There was an increase in expression of OX40, CD83 and CD29 on CD8+ T cells infiltrating Kin1-NULL tumors compared to those in Kin1-WT tumors (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: OX40, CD83 and CD29 receptors are associated with activated T cells and an increase in cytotoxic potential.
source: These receptors are associated with activated T cells and an increase in cytotoxic potential (Willoughby et al., 2017; Hirano, 2006; Nicolet et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Willoughby et al., 2017; Hirano, 2006; Nicolet et al., 2020.

claim: Analysis of CD107a expression (degranulation marker) and Granzyme B expression (cytotoxic granule) demonstrated a marked and significant increase in expression of these two markers on CD8+ effector T cells in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: To confirm this, analysis of CD107a expression (degranulation marker) and Granzyme B expression (cytotoxic granule) demonstrated a marked and significant increase in expression of these two markers on CD8+ effector T cells in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 causes a reduction in Treg suppressive function, which can enhance the activation of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, leading to reduced tumor growth.
source: Together, these data suggest that loss of Kindlin-1 causes a reduction in Treg suppressive function, which can enhance the activation of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, leading to reduced tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in Treg and CD8+ T cell phenotypes.

claim: Analysis of Tgfb ligands showed a significant increase in Tgfb2 but not Tgfb1 or Tgfb3 in the Kin1-NULL cells.
source: Analysis of Tgfb ligands showed a significant increase in Tgfb2 but not Tgfb1 or Tgfb3 in the Kin1-NULL cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The increase in Tgfb2 was not seen in analysis of bulk tumors.
source: The increase in Tgb2 was not seen in analysis of bulk tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no difference in phospho-SMAD3 between the Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors indicating that the TGF-β-SMAD signaling pathway is not altered.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in phospho-SMAD3 between the Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors indicating that the TGF-β-SMAD signaling pathway is not altered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Decreases in CXCL11, 12 and IL-12 and significant increases in CXCL13, IL-1RA, and IL-6 were detected in conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells compared to Kin1-WT and Kin1-AA cells.
source: Decreases in CXCL11, 12 and IL-12 and significant increases in CXCL13, IL-1RA, and IL-6 were detected in conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells compared to Kin1-WT and Kin1-AA cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by forward phase protein array data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The increase in secretion of IL-6 protein in conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells was confirmed by ELISA.
source: The increase in secretion of IL-6 protein in conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells was confirmed by ELISA (Figure 5B), while bulk tumor RNA analysis of Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors showed changes in IL-6-related genes, with an increase in Il6, Il6ra, and Il6st found in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Bulk tumor RNA analysis of Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors showed changes in IL-6-related genes, with an increase in Il6, Il6ra, and Il6st found in Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: The increase in secretion of IL-6 protein in conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells was confirmed by ELISA (Figure 5B), while bulk tumor RNA analysis of Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL tumors showed changes in IL-6-related genes, with an increase in Il6, Il6ra, and Il6st found in Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Analysis of Il6 in Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL cells in vitro showed no difference in expression indicating that Kindlin-1 is not regulating transcription of Il6 in the tumor cells themselves.
source: However, analysis of Il6 in Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL cells in vitro showed no difference in expression indicating that Kindlin-1 is not regulating transcription of Il6 in the tumor cells themselves (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of Cxcl13 was not altered between the Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL cells.
source: Interestingly expression of Cxcl13 was also not altered between the Kin1-WT and Kin1-NULL cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The altered cytokine profile secreted by Kin1-NULL cells is able to modulate signaling within local immune microenvironments.
source: Overall, this suggests that the altered cytokine profile secreted by Kin1-NULL cells is able to modulate signaling within local immune microenvironments.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in cytokine secretion and immune cell phenotypes.

claim: Conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells resulted in a reduction of differentiation of CD4+ T cells into FoxP3+ Tregs compared to that seen following incubation with conditioned media from Kin1-WT cells.
source: Conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells resulted in a reduction of differentiation of CD4+ T cells into FoxP3+ Tregs compared to that seen following incubation with conditioned media from Kin1-WT cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro differentiation assay data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells in which Il6 was deleted was not able to reduce the differentiation of the CD4+ T cells into FoxP3+ Tregs.
source: We then generated Kin1-NULL cells in which Il6 was deleted using CRISPR-Cas9. This resulted in a complete block of IL-6 secretion (Figure 6C), and conditioned media from these cells was not able to reduce the differentiation of the CD4+ T cells into FoxP3+ Tregs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro differentiation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Blocking CXCL13 did not affect Treg differentiation.
source: Furthermore, blocking CXCL13 did not affect Treg differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that IL-6 is the main component in the conditioned media driving this change.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro differentiation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IL-6 is the main component in the conditioned media driving the change in Treg differentiation.
source: Furthermore, blocking CXCL13 did not affect Treg differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that IL-6 is the main component in the conditioned media driving this change.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CXCL13 blocking and IL-6 deletion experiments.

claim: The decrease in CD4+FoxP3+ cells following treatment with conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells was accompanied by an increase in CD107a and TNFα expression by CD4+ FoxP3- cells.
source: The decrease in CD4+FoxP3+ cells following treatment with conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells was accompanied by an increase in CD107a and TNFα expression by CD4+ FoxP3- cells, suggesting an increase in their activation and function (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: A corresponding increase in CD4+RoRγT+ Th17 cells was demonstrated following treatment with conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells.
source: Furthermore, a corresponding increase in CD4+RoRγT+ Th17 cells (Figure 6G) was demonstrated, implying that the conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells is diverting naïve CD4+ differentiation towards a more Th17 cell than Treg cell phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells is diverting naïve CD4+ differentiation towards a more Th17 cell than Treg cell phenotype.
source: Furthermore, a corresponding increase in CD4+RoRγT+ Th17 cells (Figure 6G) was demonstrated, implying that the conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells is diverting naïve CD4+ differentiation towards a more Th17 cell than Treg cell phenotype.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed increase in Th17 cells and decrease in Tregs.

claim: There was a significant increase in Th17 associated gene, Rorc, in Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT.
source: When we looked at RNA expression in CD45+ cells isolated from Kin1-NULL and Kin1-WT tumors, we found a significant increase in Th17 associated gene, Rorc (Ruan et al., 2011), in Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT (Figure 6H) supporting a role for Kindlin-1 in modulating CD4+ T cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Kindlin-1 plays a role in modulating CD4+ T cell differentiation.
source: When we looked at RNA expression in CD45+ cells isolated from Kin1-NULL and Kin1-WT tumors, we found a significant increase in Th17 associated gene, Rorc (Ruan et al., 2011), in Kin1-NULL tumors compared to Kin1-WT (Figure 6H) supporting a role for Kindlin-1 in modulating CD4+ T cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in Treg and Th17 differentiation.

claim: Conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells lead to a decrease in Treg suppressive capacity, shown as an increase in percentage of divided CD8+ T cells compared to incubation with Kin1-WT conditioned media.
source: Conditioned media from Kin1-NULL cells lead to a decrease in Treg suppressive capacity, shown as an increase in percentage of divided CD8+ T cells compared to incubation with Kin1-WT conditioned media (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Treg suppression assay data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Treatment with an antibody that blocks the function of IL-6 reduced the ability of conditioned media from Kin1-NULL to increase division of CD8+ T cells.
source: Treatment with an antibody that blocks the function of IL-6 reduced the ability of conditioned media from Kin1-NULL to increase division of CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Treg suppression assay data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Loss of Kindlin1 in the Met-1 cells leads to increased secretion of IL-6, which in turn reduces the ability of Tregs to suppress CD8+ T cell proliferation.
source: Thus, loss of Kindlin1 in the Met-1 cells leads to increased secretion of IL-6, which in turn reduces the ability of Tregs to suppress CD8+ T cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IL-6 blocking experiment in the Treg suppression assay.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of CD4+ T cells and Tregs in the IL-6-depleted tumors.
source: There was a significant increase in the number of CD4+ T cells and Tregs in the IL-6-depleted tumors indicating that the tumor cell derived increase in IL-6 secretion following Kindlin-1 loss can drive changes in Tregs in vivo (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The tumor cell derived increase in IL-6 secretion following Kindlin-1 loss can drive changes in Tregs in vivo.
source: There was a significant increase in the number of CD4+ T cells and Tregs in the IL-6-depleted tumors indicating that the tumor cell derived increase in IL-6 secretion following Kindlin-1 loss can drive changes in Tregs in vivo (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed reversal of Treg reduction upon IL-6 deletion.

claim: Deletion of IL-6 in Kin1-NULL tumors resulted in a significant decrease in CD107a+ Granzyme B+ CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, deletion of IL-6 in Kin1-NULL tumors resulted in a significant decrease in CD107a+ Granzyme B+ CD8+ T cells, suggesting their effector functions are impaired (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Deletion of IL-6 in Kin1-NULL tumors was not sufficient to prevent clearance of the Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: However, this was not sufficient to prevent clearance of the Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Treatment with an IL-6 blocking antibody was not able to prevent clearance of the Kin1-NULL tumors.
source: In addition, treatment with an IL-6 blocking antibody was not able to prevent clearance of the Kin1-NULL tumors (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Depletion of CD25+ cells resulted in depletion of CD4+ FoxP3+, but not CD4+ FoxP3- T cells, demonstrating deletion of Tregs.
source: Although expression of CD25 is not specific to Tregs, it is a cell surface protein that has been widely used to deplete Treg cells (Hayes et al., 2020; Clemente-Casares et al., 2016; Göschl et al., 2018), and anti-CD25 antibody treatment resulted in depletion of CD4+ FoxP3+, but not CD4+ FoxP3- T cells, demonstrating deletion of Tregs, due to their high and constitutive expression of CD25 (Peng et al., 2023; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of CD25+ cells resulted in a reduction of tumor growth compared to controls.
source: Depletion of CD25+ cells resulted in a reduction of tumor growth compared to controls (Figure 7F), demonstrating a similar growth pattern as seen in Kin-1 NULL tumors (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There was a significant reduction in tumor size at Day 17 in Kin1-WT tumors with depleted Tregs.
source: There was a significant reduction in tumor size at Day 17 (Figure 7G) in Kin1-WT tumors with depleted Tregs.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor size data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Treg-mediated immune suppression is important in Kin1-WT tumors, leading to an increase in tumor growth.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate the importance of Treg-mediated immune suppression in Kin1-WT tumors, leading to an increase in tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Treg depletion experiment results.

claim: The Kindlin-1-dependent regulation of IL-6 secretion from the Met-1 tumor cells was able to regulate Treg infiltration and the function of the cytotoxic T cells in vivo.
source: Although the Kindlin-1-dependent regulation of IL-6 secretion from the Met-1 tumor cells was able to able to regulate Treg infiltration and the function of the cytotoxic T cells in vivo this was not sufficient to induce tumor clearance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the IL-6 deletion and blocking experiments.

claim: The Kindlin-1-dependent regulation of IL-6 secretion was not sufficient to induce tumor clearance.
source: Although the Kindlin-1-dependent regulation of IL-6 secretion from the Met-1 tumor cells was able to able to regulate Treg infiltration and the function of the cytotoxic T cells in vivo this was not sufficient to induce tumor clearance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that IL-6 deletion/blocking did not prevent tumor clearance.

claim: Kindlin-1 can regulate breast cancer progression by modulating the anti-tumor immune response through regulation of the immune composition of the tumor microenvironment.
source: Here we show that Kindlin-1 can also regulate breast cancer progression by modulating the anti-tumor immune response through regulation of the immune composition of the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: The ability of Kindlin-1 to bind integrins is not required for the growth of Met-1 tumors, or their immune clearance in immunocompetent animals.
source: We show that the ability of Kindlin-1 to bind integrins is not required for the growth of Met-1 tumors, or their immune clearance in immunocompetent animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Kin1-AA tumor growth data.

claim: The secretion of both IL-6 and CXCL13 was not altered by the ability of Kindlin-1 to bind β1 integrins.
source: Furthermore, the secretion of both IL-6 and CXCL13 was not altered by the ability of Kindlin-1 to bind β1 integrins, supporting a role for secreted cytokines in driving the integrin-independent immune changes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein array data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Redundancy between Kindlin-1 and Kindlin-2 has been reported in relation to integrin-dependent functions.
source: Redundancy between Kindlin-1 and Kindlin-2 has been reported in relation to integrin-dependent functions, where they have overlapping roles (Azorin et al., 2018; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Azorin et al., 2018 and He et al., 2011.

claim: There was no change in Kindlin-2 expression following depletion of Kindlin-1 in the Met-1 cell line model.
source: However, in the Met-1 cell line model we used here, we saw no change in Kindlin-2 expression following depletion of Kindlin-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), implying that an increase in Kindlin-2 is not driving the effects on immune cell populations and anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in Kindlin-2 is not driving the effects on immune cell populations and anti-tumor immunity in the Met-1 model.
source: However, in the Met-1 cell line model we used here, we saw no change in Kindlin-2 expression following depletion of Kindlin-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), implying that an increase in Kindlin-2 is not driving the effects on immune cell populations and anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of change in Kindlin-2 expression.

claim: Kindlin-2 has been reported to control the recruitment of immunosuppressive (F4/80+, CD206+) macrophages in orthotopic breast cancer models.
source: Interestingly, Kindlin-2 has been reported to control the recruitment of immunosuppressive (F4/80+, CD206+) macrophages in orthotopic breast cancer models; Kindlin-2 in the tumor cells is required for the secretion of colony-stimulating factor-1 that acts as a chemoattractant for the macrophages (Sossey-Alaoui et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sossey-Alaoui et al., 2017.

claim: FAK is important in regulating anti-tumor immunity, which is driven in part by transcriptional regulation of cytokine production.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated the importance of the focal adhesion protein FAK in regulating anti-tumor immunity (Serrels et al., 2015; Canel et al., 2020; Serrels et al., 2017), which is driven in part by transcriptional regulation of cytokine production.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Serrels et al., 2015; Canel et al., 2020; Serrels et al., 2017.

claim: For IL-6 (and CXCL13) Kindlin-1 regulation is not controlled at the level of transcription.
source: Here we show that Kindlin-1 can also alter cytokine production leading to changes in the immune environment. However, for IL-6 (and CXCL13) this is not controlled at the level of transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that Il6 and Cxcl13 mRNA levels are not changed in Kin1-NULL cells.

claim: Il6 is primarily regulated via transcription.
source: Although Il6 is primarily regulated via transcription the secretion of IL-6 is also regulated by other processes including via trafficking through the endocytic pathway (Revelo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Revelo et al., 2019 and general knowledge.

claim: The secretion of IL-6 is also regulated by other processes including via trafficking through the endocytic pathway.
source: Although Il6 is primarily regulated via transcription the secretion of IL-6 is also regulated by other processes including via trafficking through the endocytic pathway (Revelo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Revelo et al., 2019.

claim: Kindlin-dependent regulation of integrin trafficking has been reported.
source: Further studies are required to establish how Kindlin regulates IL-6 secretion, although Kindlin-dependent regulation of integrin trafficking has been reported (Margadant et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Margadant et al., 2012.

claim: IL-6 secretion is increased from keratinocytes from Kindler syndrome patients that lack Kindlin-1.
source: Of note is the observation that IL-6 secretion is also increased from keratinocytes from Kindler syndrome patients that lack Kindlin-1 (Maier et al., 2016; Qu et al., 2012), although its function is not known.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 2016 and Qu et al., 2012.

claim: IL-6 has well-known pro-tumorigenic roles.
source: Although IL-6 has well-known pro-tumorigenic roles, a number of studies have demonstrated the importance of IL-6 in reducing Treg suppressive function in various settings (Guo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2019), and also in the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Tregs (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by general knowledge.

claim: A number of studies have demonstrated the importance of IL-6 in reducing Treg suppressive function in various settings.
source: Although IL-6 has well-known pro-tumorigenic roles, a number of studies have demonstrated the importance of IL-6 in reducing Treg suppressive function in various settings (Guo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2019), and also in the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Tregs (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2019.

claim: IL-6 is important in the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Tregs.
source: Although IL-6 has well-known pro-tumorigenic roles, a number of studies have demonstrated the importance of IL-6 in reducing Treg suppressive function in various settings (Guo et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2019), and also in the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Tregs (Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kimura and Kishimoto, 2010.

claim: Granzyme B is an important cytotoxic molecule secreted alongside Perforin in granules by activated CD8+ T cells in order to induce apoptosis of target cells.
source: As Granzyme B is an important cytotoxic molecule secreted alongside Perforin in granules by activated CD8+ T cells in order to induce apoptosis of target cells (Voskoboinik et al., 2015), these data imply that Kindlin-1 can impair the ability of T cells to mediate tumor cell killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voskoboinik et al., 2015.

claim: Kindlin-1 can impair the ability of T cells to mediate tumor cell killing.
source: As Granzyme B is an important cytotoxic molecule secreted alongside Perforin in granules by activated CD8+ T cells in order to induce apoptosis of target cells (Voskoboinik et al., 2015), these data imply that Kindlin-1 can impair the ability of T cells to mediate tumor cell killing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed reduction in Granzyme B and CD107a upon IL-6 deletion.

claim: The inability of IL-6 blockade to impact on the clearance of Kin1-NULL tumors means that other mechanisms of immune regulation are also involved.
source: However, the inability of IL-6 blockade to impact on the clearance of Kin1-NULL tumors means that other mechanisms of immune regulation are also involved.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that IL-6 blocking did not prevent tumor clearance.

claim: Loss of Kindlin-1 impacts several immune cell types that are known to contribute to anti-tumor immunity.
source: Thus, loss of Kindlin-1 impacts several immune cell types that are known to contribute to anti-tumor immunity and future studies will explore how other factors act in concert with IL-6 to drive anti-tumor immunity in response to Kindlin-1 depletion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in Tregs, cDC1s, and CD8+ T cells.

claim: Kindlin-1 is upregulated in breast cancer and linked to survival.
source: As Kindlin-1 is upregulated in breast cancer and linked to survival, targeting Kindlin-1-dependent pathways linked to immune phenotypes may provide a novel strategy to increase the efficacy of immunotherapies in breast cancer, particularly methods relating to reinvigorating the anti-tumor T cell response.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior citations in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting Kindlin-1-dependent pathways linked to immune phenotypes may provide a novel strategy to increase the efficacy of immunotherapies in breast cancer.
source: As Kindlin-1 is upregulated in breast cancer and linked to survival, targeting Kindlin-1-dependent pathways linked to immune phenotypes may provide a novel strategy to increase the efficacy of immunotherapies in breast cancer, particularly methods relating to reinvigorating the anti-tumor T cell response.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the study findings.
